study.title: Zechariah 5 - the flying roller and the efa of the perversity
study.overview: This chapter presents two visions that are completed. In the first, a flying scroll announces that the curse of the covenant continues to act against theft and the false oath; God attains sin within the houses and destroys it. In the second, an ephah with a woman named "Perversity" shows that evil is being removed from the midst of the people and led away, toward the land of Sinar. The whole teaches that God not only restores, but also purifies, judging sin and distancing them from his people.

outline.title: The flying roll and the curse of the covenant
outline.explanation: Zechariah sees a scroll flying through the air, a visible sign of judgment. The text itself explains that it represents the curse against the thief and against whom it vows falsely. The punishment does not lie at the level of the speech: it enters the house of the guilty and knocks it completely.

outline.title: The epha, the woman and the contained perversity
outline.explanation: The angel presents a second sign: a container of measurement, associated with God's gaze on the earth. Inside it is a woman identified as Perversity, which is pushed down and sealed with a lead cap. The picture shows the evil being contained and removed under divine authority.

outline.title: The Perversity taken to Sinar
outline.explanation: Two winged women take the efa to the land of Sinar, where a house will be built. The final movement indicates displacement out of the earth, fixing evil in its place of origin or historical association with rebellion, rather than leaving it among the people of God.

study.context: The notes associate the first vision with the post-exile period in Judah, when the people still needed to remember that the demands of the law remained in force. Tyndale notes that the curse of the scroll echoes the blessings and curses of the covenant, and that the second vision continues the theme of purification initiated before in the book. The notes also identify Sinar as Babylon, linked to captivity, and, in later readings, symbol of systems opposite God.
study.theology: The chapter highlights the holiness of God and its active action against sin. The theft and the false oath appear as central violations of the covenant: one against the neighbor and the other against the name of the Lord. The image of the scroll teaches that divine judgment is comprehensive and penetrates into the house of the guilty. The ephaly with the woman shows that perversity is not only forgiven; she is removed, restrained and sent away. Thus God appears as the one that purges his evil people, preserving the covenant and separating them from unrighteousness. The readings of the commentators vary as to the historical reach of these visions, but they all treat the chapter as an announcement of God's action against impiety.

scholarViews.insight: The vision of the flying scroll reminds the post-exile leaders and people of Judah who remained bound by the commandments of God; the curse of the covenant was still in force.
The image of the flying scroll shows that God also proclaims judgment against the rebels, and not only peace; the vision has a dark side for those who persist in sin.
The woman in the epha can represent the wickedness, and the women who carry it indicate the removal of evil away from the people, with the weight of lead symbolizing their containment.

questions: What kinds of sin does the chapter specially highlight, and why false theft and oath are presented together?
What does the image of God entering the house of the guilty teach about the seriousness of hidden sin?
How does the removal of "Perversity" help to understand that the restoration of God also includes purification?
study.practice: Read this chapter as a call to concrete repentance. Examine words, business, and promises made in the name of God; reject any form of dishonesty. At the same time, ask the Lord not only to forgive, but also to remove from his life what he defiles. Practice visible integrity at home, at work and in the church, remembering that God sees and acts both in the public and in hiding.
study.uncertainty: The notes do not agree on the exact scope of the visions: some understand them as warnings to the people of Judah, others as a broader reference to Babylon or to later historical outcomes. There is also a distinct symbolic reading of the woman in the epha and on the land of Sinar. Therefore, interpretations should be read as exegetical possibilities, not as absolute certainties of the text.
